answer: Yes. The private router (`private.router`, the endpoints in routes/private.py) is only mounted when `settings.ENVIRONMENT == "local"`. The other routers (login, users, utils, items) are always mounted.

Make sure the PR has exactly one of these labels: breaking, security, feature, bug, refactor, upgrade, docs, lang-all, or internal. The label-checker step uses `one_of`. It fails if the PR has none of them, and the `one_of` rule also means it shouldn't have more than one. The labeler action may add a label automatically. If it doesn't, add one by hand. The check re-runs when you label or unlabel the PR.

Operation IDs are generated by `custom_generate_unique_id` in the backend. It's passed to FastAPI as `generate_unique_id_function`, and it returns `"{first tag}-{route function name}"`. For example, a route function `read_items` tagged `items` gets the ID `items-read_items`. Every route therefore needs at least one tag, because the function reads `route.tags[0]`.

On the frontend, `openapi-ts.config.ts` uses these IDs to build the client. The tag becomes the service class, named `{{name}}Service` (for example `ItemsService`). `methodNameBuilder` removes the service-name prefix from the operation name if it's there, and lowercases the first letter. The result is a method like `ItemsService.readItems`.

Publishing a GitHub release (release event, type `published`) triggers the "Deploy to Production" workflow. It runs on a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner labeled `production`. The job is skipped when the repository owner is `fastapi`, so it only runs in user projects.
90% minimum backend coverage. The backend test workflow runs `coverage report --fail-under=90`, so CI fails below that. The smokeshow workflow also sets a coverage threshold of 90.
8 days (ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES = 60 * 24 * 8 = 11520 minutes). The login route uses this value when it creates the access token.

A local pre-commit hook, `add-release-date`, runs whenever release-notes.md changes. It runs `uv run python scripts/add_latest_release_date.py`. That script finds the first (latest) `## X.Y.Z` heading. If the heading has no `(…)` suffix, it rewrites the heading as `## X.Y.Z (YYYY-MM-DD)` using `date.today().isoformat()`. If the heading already has a date, it leaves it alone.

A pydantic model validator in the Settings class (`_enforce_non_default_secrets`) checks SECRET_KEY, POSTGRES_PASSWORD and FIRST_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD via `_check_default_secret`. If any is still "changethis", it raises a ValueError whenever ENVIRONMENT isn't "local", so the app won't start. In the local environment it only emits a warning.

Startup fails. With ENVIRONMENT=staging and SECRET_KEY="changethis", the Settings model validator `_enforce_non_default_secrets` calls `_check_default_secret`. That raises a ValueError: 'The value of SECRET_KEY is "changethis", for security, please change it, at least for deployments.' Because `settings = Settings()` runs at import, the app won't boot. Only ENVIRONMENT=local gets a warning instead. The same check applies to POSTGRES_PASSWORD and FIRST_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD.

The backend pre-start database check (run by prestart.sh) makes up to 300 attempts (max_tries = 60 * 5, about 5 minutes). It waits a fixed 1 second between attempts (wait_seconds = 1, using tenacity's wait_fixed).

No. A superuser can't delete their own account through the users endpoints. DELETE /users/me returns 403 "Super users are not allowed to delete themselves" when current_user.is_superuser is true. The admin delete-by-id endpoint, around line 226, returns the same 403 error.
You need at least 90% total coverage. The backend CI job runs `coverage report --fail-under=90`, so it fails if coverage is below 90%. The separate smokeshow workflow also uses a threshold of 90.

The operationId will be "orders-<function_name>", which is the first tag, a hyphen, and the endpoint function's name. For example, a function named `read_orders` gets "orders-read_orders". `custom_generate_unique_id` builds it as f"{route.tags[0]}-{route.name}", and the FastAPI app uses it through `generate_unique_id_function`.

GET /items/ returns an ItemsPublic object, `{data: [...], count: N}`. A normal user gets only the items they own (`Item.owner_id == current_user.id`), and `count` is the number of their own items. A superuser gets every item from all owners, and `count` is the total number of items. For both, items are sorted by `created_at` descending, so the newest come first. Pagination uses `skip` (default 0) and `limit` (default 100). `count` is the total number of matching items, not the number on the page.

The token is kept in the browser's localStorage under the key "access_token". useAuth.ts writes it at login (line 45), and main.tsx supplies it to the API client through OpenAPI.TOKEN. When any query or mutation fails with an ApiError whose status is 401 or 403, handleApiError removes "access_token" from localStorage and redirects the browser to /login with window.location.href.

The generated client only contains PrivateService if it was generated from an OpenAPI schema produced with ENVIRONMENT == "local". The backend registers the private router only in that environment. If the client was generated against a non-local backend (staging or production), the private routes aren't in the schema, so src/client has no PrivateService. The e2e import of it would then fail.
8 days. ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES is 60 * 24 * 8 = 11,520 minutes, and login.py uses it as the access token's expiry.

From the project root run `bash ./scripts/generate-client.sh` (with the backend virtualenv active), then commit the changes. The script: (1) cd's into backend and uses `uv run python` to import app.main and dump `app.openapi()` as JSON to openapi.json; (2) moves openapi.json into frontend/; (3) runs `bun run --filter frontend generate-client`, which runs `openapi-ts` (@hey-api/openapi-ts, configured in frontend/openapi-ts.config.ts with input ./openapi.json) to regenerate frontend/src/client; (4) runs `bun run lint` (biome) to format the generated code. Manual alternative: download /api/v1/openapi.json to frontend/openapi.json and run `bun run generate-client`.

Yes. In corpus/frontend/playwright.config.ts, the `CI` environment variable changes five settings. On CI: `forbidOnly` is true, so a committed `test.only` fails the run. Retries are 2 locally 0. Workers are limited to 1 (locally Playwright picks its default). The reporter is 'blob' (locally 'html'). `reuseExistingServer` is false, so the web server is always started fresh (locally an already-running server is reused). The `retries` setting is at line 19, and the other four are at lines 17, 21, 23 and 89.

An admin (superuser) sees everybody's items, not just their own. The endpoint doesn't filter by owner for superusers, and the count covers all items. Regular users only get items where owner_id matches their own id. In both cases the items come back newest first, ordered by created_at descending. They're paginated with skip=0 and limit=100 by default.

The /admin route has a TanStack Router `beforeLoad` guard that fetches the current user (UsersService.readUserMe()) and, if `!user.is_superuser`, throws `redirect({ to: "/" })`, sending non-superusers to the home page. The sidebar (AppSidebar.tsx) also only shows the Admin link when `currentUser.is_superuser`.

Traefik routes by Host rule in corpus/compose.yml: backend → api.${DOMAIN}, frontend → dashboard.${DOMAIN}, Adminer → adminer.${DOMAIN}. Each has both an http and an https router. (The Traefik dashboard itself is traefik.${DOMAIN} in compose.traefik.yml.)
The backend service runs `curl -f http://localhost:8000/api/v1/utils/health-check/` as its healthcheck (`test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", ...]`). It runs every 10s with a 5s timeout and 5 retries.

Give the runner the label `production`. It also gets the default `self-hosted` label, and the deploy job requires both. The job is handed to it by a GitHub `release` event of type `published`, meaning you publish a release. The job is skipped if the repository owner is `fastapi`.
About 5 minutes: it retries once per second for up to 300 attempts (60*5) before failing.
By default the backend image runs `fastapi run --workers 4 app/main.py`, which is the FastAPI app served in production mode with 4 workers.
With CI set, Playwright uses the 'blob' reporter (needed so shard reports can be merged) and 2 retries. Without CI it uses the 'html' reporter and 0 retries.
Run `docker compose watch` from the repo root. The frontend ends up at http://localhost:5173 and the backend API at http://localhost:8000. Swagger docs are at http://localhost:8000/docs.

Traefik gets its certificates from Let's Encrypt through an ACME certificate resolver named "le". The resolver is configured with the EMAIL env var and uses the TLS-ALPN challenge (`tlschallenge=true`). Routers opt in with the label `tls.certresolver=le`. The certificates are stored in `/certificates/acme.json`. That path is on the named Docker volume `traefik-public-certificates`, so they persist when the container is recreated.

The browser keeps your session as a JWT in localStorage under the key "access_token". It's written on login in useAuth.ts:45 and read for every API request in main.tsx:18. Two things send you back to /login. (1) The global React Query error handler in main.tsx:21-25 catches any API response with status 401 or 403. It deletes access_token and sets window.location.href = "/login". A 401 or 403 usually means the token expired (the backend default is 8 days, ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES = 60*24*8) or was rejected. (2) The _layout.tsx route guard (line 15) redirects to login when isLoggedIn() finds no access_token in localStorage. Logging out (useAuth.ts:57) also removes the token.

A password-reset link is valid for 48 hours (EMAIL_RESET_TOKEN_EXPIRE_HOURS = 48). It opens the frontend's /reset-password page, with the token in the query string: {FRONTEND_HOST}/reset-password?token=...

Open the Mailcatcher web UI at http://localhost:1080. Locally, Docker Compose runs a Mailcatcher container. The backend sends its emails (including password recovery) to it over SMTP on port 1025 instead of to real recipients. The captured emails appear in that web interface.

The Admin sidebar item only appears for superusers. AppSidebar.tsx adds it only when currentUser.is_superuser is true, so your account isn't a superuser. If you go to /admin anyway, the route's beforeLoad fetches your user with UsersService.readUserMe(). Because is_superuser is false, it throws a redirect to "/", the home page, so you never see the Admin page. The backend also enforces this. Its superuser check in deps.py returns an error for non-superusers, so the users API is protected as well.

After deploying, open the dashboard (frontend) at https://dashboard.<DOMAIN> and the API at https://api.<DOMAIN>. For example, with DOMAIN=fastapi-project.example.com, the dashboard is https://dashboard.fastapi-project.example.com and the API base URL is https://api.fastapi-project.example.com. The API docs are at https://api.fastapi-project.example.com/docs. Staging works the same way under a staging subdomain, e.g. https://dashboard.staging.fastapi-project.example.com.
docker compose exec backend bash scripts/tests-start.sh  (extra pytest args can be appended, e.g. -x)

No. The /password-recovery/{email} endpoint returns the same message whether or not the account exists: "If that email is registered, we sent a password recovery link". The email is only sent if the user exists. The separate superuser-only /password-recovery-html-content/ endpoint does return a 404 for unknown emails, but it requires superuser authentication.

We use Argon2 (via pwdlib), which is the first and default hasher. Bcrypt is kept only as a legacy verifier. Accounts with old bcrypt hashes still log in normally. On a successful login, `verify_and_update` returns a new Argon2 hash. `authenticate` saves it to the user's `hashed_password` and commits. Accounts that never log in keep their bcrypt hashes. Argon2 hashes are left unchanged.

Largely no. authenticate() runs verify_password against a DUMMY_HASH (Argon2) when the email isn't found, so unknown and known emails take similar time, and the route returns the same generic "Incorrect email or password" error. Only negligible residual differences remain (DB lookup, rehash on legacy bcrypt success).

No. Sentry is only initialised when SENTRY_DSN is set and ENVIRONMENT is not "local". ENVIRONMENT defaults to "local" for development, so local backend runs don't send errors to Sentry. The exception is a developer who sets ENVIRONMENT to something else, such as staging or production, together with a DSN.

A staging deployment is triggered by a push (or merge) to the `master` branch. The "Deploy to Staging" GitHub Actions workflow runs on a self-hosted runner labelled `staging`. It doesn't run in the main `fastapi` repository, only in user projects. The job builds and starts the stack with `docker compose` (`build`, then `up -d`).

Dependabot checks GitHub Actions daily. It checks the uv (Python), bun (frontend), Docker (/backend and /frontend) and Docker Compose ecosystems weekly. The only exclusion is the bun ecosystem, which ignores the `@hey-api/openapi-ts` dependency.

The suite is split into 4 parallel shards. A matrix on `test-playwright` sets shardIndex 1–4 and shardTotal 4, with fail-fast off. Each shard runs `playwright test --shard=N/4` inside docker compose and uploads a blob report. A `merge-playwright-reports` job then combines those into one HTML report. It runs even if some shards failed. The suite doesn't run at all when a `changes` job (a dorny/paths-filter step) finds no changes in `backend/**`, `frontend/**`, `.env`, `compose*.yml` or `.github/workflows/playwright.yml`. In that case `test-playwright` is skipped, and the `alls-green` check allows that skip. The workflow only triggers on pushes to master, on pull requests when they are opened or synchronized, and on manual dispatch.

The API accepts cross-origin requests from the origins listed in the BACKEND_CORS_ORIGINS setting (a comma-separated list, with trailing slashes stripped). It also always accepts FRONTEND_HOST, which defaults to http://localhost:5173. These are combined in `all_cors_origins` and passed to CORSMiddleware as `allow_origins` in main.py. If `all_cors_origins` is empty the middleware is not added, but it always contains FRONTEND_HOST.

The backend lint script runs four checks on `app`. They are mypy type checking (`mypy app`), ty type checking (`ty check app`), ruff lint rules (`ruff check app`), and a ruff format check (`ruff format app --check`) that fails on unformatted code without rewriting it.

The session token is not in an httpOnly cookie. It is stored in `localStorage` under the key `access_token`, so any JavaScript on the page can read it. The backend returns it in the login response body, and the frontend writes it to `localStorage` after login (useAuth.ts:45). The only cookie I found is the sidebar UI-state cookie, which has nothing to do with auth.

It is wiped in two cases:
1. **Logout:** `logout()` calls `localStorage.removeItem("access_token")` and then navigates to /login (useAuth.ts:57).
2. **Auth failure:** any API response with status 401 or 403 makes the global error handler remove the token and redirect to /login (main.tsx:22-24).

I found no expiry or cleanup on the client beyond these two. The token otherwise persists across browser restarts until it is removed this way. I did not check the backend's JWT lifetime.
UUIDs. Models define `id: uuid.UUID = Field(default_factory=uuid.uuid4, primary_key=True)` for both User and Item. An Alembic migration (d98dd8ec85a3) converted the old integer IDs to UUIDs.

The user's items are deleted along with the user (cascade delete). User.items is declared with cascade_delete=True and Item.owner_id is a foreign key with ondelete="CASCADE". The admin delete endpoint also explicitly deletes the user's Items before deleting the user.

Production certificates are issued by Let's Encrypt. Traefik uses the ACME resolver "le" with the TLS challenge, and the contact email comes from the EMAIL variable. Traefik writes the certificates to /certificates/acme.json. That path is on the named volume `traefik-public-certificates`, so recreating the Traefik container does not lose them. They are lost only if the volume itself is deleted.

It raises an HTTPException with status 403 Forbidden and detail "Could not validate credentials". This happens when jwt.decode raises InvalidTokenError (expired or tampered token) or the payload fails TokenPayload validation.

If SECRET_KEY isn't set in the environment/.env, Settings uses a randomly generated value, `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`. It is created fresh each time the process starts. The README's documented default of "changethis" doesn't match the code. config.py line 110 also runs `_check_default_secret` on the key, which checks for that "changethis" placeholder.

After a successful login, the bcrypt hash is replaced with an upgraded Argon2 hash. `verify_password` calls pwdlib's `verify_and_update`, which returns a new hash for legacy hashes. `authenticate` then sets `db_user.hashed_password` to that hash, commits it and refreshes the user. A failed login leaves the old hash unchanged.

Defaults (config.py): SMTP_TLS=True, SMTP_SSL=False, SMTP_PORT=587, SMTP_HOST/USER/PASSWORD=None, EMAILS_FROM_EMAIL/NAME=None. (compose.override.yml sets SMTP_TLS to "false" for the local mail catcher.) If both SMTP_TLS and SMTP_SSL are true, TLS wins: send_email in utils.py uses `if settings.SMTP_TLS: ... elif settings.SMTP_SSL:`, so only tls=True is set and SSL is ignored.

Every password field in the request models has a minimum length of 8 and a maximum length of 128 characters. This covers UserCreate.password, UserRegister.password, UserUpdate.password (optional), UpdatePassword.current_password and new_password, and the new_password field at line 129 (the reset-password body, I think). I didn't open line 129 to confirm which model it belongs to.

The `emails_enabled` computed property on the settings decides it. It returns true only when both `SMTP_HOST` and `EMAILS_FROM_EMAIL` are set. `send_email` in `utils.py` asserts it, and the user-creation route checks it before sending a welcome email.

It rejects the request with HTTP 409 Conflict and the detail "User with this email already exists". The check looks up the new email and fails if it belongs to a different user. Nothing is saved in that case. Setting your own current email doesn't trigger the error.

A 403 Forbidden response with the body {"detail": "Not enough permissions"}. GET, PUT and DELETE on /items/{id} all do the same check. If the item doesn't exist, they return 404 "Item not found" instead. Superusers skip the ownership check.

PATCH /users/me/password returns HTTP 400 in two cases. The first is "Incorrect password", when current_password doesn't match the stored hash. The second is "New password cannot be the same as the current one", when the new password equals the current one. Two more errors come from outside the handler's own code. A missing or invalid auth token is rejected by the CurrentUser dependency, and a body that fails the UpdatePassword schema returns a 422 validation error. I didn't open the dependency or the schema, so those two are not confirmed from the code.

Yes. POST /api/v1/users/signup (register_user) is public and needs no login. If the email is already registered, it raises HTTPException 400 with detail "The user with this email already exists in the system". Otherwise it creates the user and returns UserPublic.

From the top-level project directory (with the backend virtualenv activated), run `bash ./scripts/generate-client.sh`. It dumps the app's OpenAPI schema to openapi.json, moves it into frontend/, and runs `bun run --filter frontend generate-client` (openapi-ts) to regenerate frontend/src/client. Then commit the changes. The manual alternative is to download openapi.json from http://localhost/api/v1/openapi.json into frontend/ and run `bun run generate-client`.

The recovery email is caught by the Mailcatcher container (schickling/mailcatcher) and is not delivered to a real inbox. You can read it in the Mailcatcher web UI at http://localhost:1080. compose.override.yml sets the backend's SMTP environment to SMTP_HOST=mailcatcher, SMTP_PORT=1025 and SMTP_TLS=false, with EMAILS_FROM_EMAIL=noreply@example.com. Mailcatcher's SMTP port 1025 is also published on the host. backend/app/utils.py builds its SMTP options from these settings.

A session-scoped, autouse `db` fixture in conftest.py opens a Session and runs init_db. After all tests finish, it runs `delete(Item)` and `delete(User)` and commits. This removes all rows from both tables once at the end of the session. It doesn't clean up between individual tests.

Both names come from the FastAPI backend's operation IDs, which openapi-ts then reshapes. In backend/app/main.py, `custom_generate_unique_id` returns `f"{route.tags[0]}-{route.name}"`. The `items` router has `tags=["items"]` and its function is `read_items`, so the operationId is `items-read_items`. The `@hey-api/sdk` plugin in frontend/openapi-ts.config.ts uses `asClass: true` and `operationId: true`. It groups operations by the first tag and names the class with `classNameBuilder: "{{name}}Service"`, which gives `ItemsService`. The custom `methodNameBuilder` strips the service-name prefix from the operation name if there is one and lowercases the first letter. That gives `readItems`.

The /_layout route's `beforeLoad` calls `isLoggedIn()`. If that returns false, it throws a redirect to `/login`. `isLoggedIn()` only checks that an `access_token` key exists in localStorage (`localStorage.getItem("access_token") !== null`). It does not validate the token, so it doesn't check the signature or expiry, and it doesn't call the server. A stale or bogus token still gets past the guard. The token is only checked when a later API call, such as `readUserMe`, is made with it and the backend rejects it.
If the URL has no token (missing or non-string, which the zod schema coerces to ""), the route's beforeLoad guard redirects to /login. A logged-in user is redirected to "/" before that check.

They get redirected to the home page "/". Both the /login and /signup routes have a `beforeLoad` guard. If `isLoggedIn()` is true, the guard throws `redirect({ to: "/" })`, so the form never renders. `isLoggedIn()` is a client-side check in `useAuth.ts`. I read the guard in login.tsx directly. For signup.tsx, search results show the same `isLoggedIn()` check in its route definition, but I didn't open the file to confirm it also redirects to "/".

A first-time visitor gets the "dark" theme. main.tsx wraps the app in <ThemeProvider defaultTheme="dark" storageKey="vite-ui-theme">, and that overrides the provider's own default of "system". This default is used when localStorage has no saved value. A changed theme is saved in the browser's localStorage under the key "vite-ui-theme". setTheme writes it there.

The email link is f"{settings.FRONTEND_HOST}/reset-password?token={token}". With the default FRONTEND_HOST that is http://localhost:5173/reset-password?token=<JWT>. The token is valid for EMAIL_RESET_TOKEN_EXPIRE_HOURS, which defaults to 48 hours (2 days).

The shared DataTable offers rows-per-page options of 5, 10, 25 and 50. The whole pagination footer is only rendered when `table.getPageCount() > 1`, meaning there is more than one page of data. The footer holds the "Showing X to Y of N entries" text, the rows-per-page select, the "Page X of Y" indicator and the first/previous/next/last buttons. I didn't see a `pageSize` set in the table config, so the page size is TanStack Table's default. That default is 10 as far as I know, but I didn't confirm it in this repo.

Mutations set `onError: handleError.bind(showErrorToast)`. `handleError` calls `extractErrorMessage(err)` and passes the result to `showErrorToast`, which comes from `useCustomToast`. For an AxiosError, the text is `err.message`. Otherwise it is `err.body.detail`. If `detail` is an array, the text is the first item's `.msg`. If there is no detail, the text is "Something went wrong."

After creating an item, only the ["items"] query key is invalidated (AddItem's onSettled calls invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["items"] })). After deleting an item, every cache is invalidated, because DeleteItem's onSettled calls queryClient.invalidateQueries() with no key filter. Both run in onSettled, so they happen whether the mutation succeeds or fails.

No. The code branches on `is_superuser`, but both branches give the same tabs. Superusers get `tabsConfig.slice(0, 3)` and everyone else gets `tabsConfig`. `tabsConfig` has only three entries (My profile, Password, Danger zone), so the slice returns all three. The conditional has no effect, probably left over from an earlier version that hid some tabs.
No. The profile form limits full name to 30 characters (z.string().max(30)). The API limits it to 255 (max_length=255 in the backend models).

UserActionsMenu deliberately returns null when the row's user id equals the logged-in user's id (useAuth().user). This stops admins from editing or deleting their own account from the admin table. The row is marked with a "You" badge via isCurrentUser in columns.tsx.

If the admin is a superuser, the API rejects the request. DELETE /users/me returns 403 with the detail "Super users are not allowed to delete themselves", and nothing is deleted. In the app, the mutation's onError handler runs handleError, which shows that message in an error toast. The success path, which shows "Your account has been successfully deleted" and calls logout(), is skipped. The admin stays logged in and the dialog is still open. onSettled still invalidates the currentUser query.

A non-superuser gets a different result. The API deletes the user and returns "User deleted successfully". The app then shows a success toast and logs out.

The prestart service uses the backend image and runs `bash scripts/prestart.sh`. That script runs three steps in order: `python app/backend_pre_start.py`, which waits for the DB to be up; `alembic upgrade head`, which runs the migrations; and `python app/initial_data.py`, which creates the initial data. The backend service waits for prestart to complete successfully before it starts.

The `db` service runs the `postgres:18` image. Its healthcheck is `pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER} -d ${POSTGRES_DB}`, run every 10s with a 10s timeout, 5 retries and a 30s start period. The data is in the named Docker volume `app-db-data`, mounted at `/var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata`. `PGDATA` is set to the same path.

The backend reports to Sentry in staging and production, but not in local. The init in backend/app/main.py runs only if SENTRY_DSN is set and ENVIRONMENT != "local". ENVIRONMENT can be "local", "staging" or "production", and it defaults to "local". The staging and production deploy workflows set ENVIRONMENT to staging and production respectively, and both pass SENTRY_DSN from secrets. If the secret is empty in either one, Sentry stays off there. Both deploy workflows read the same SENTRY_DSN secret, so staging and production will report to the same Sentry project.

The frontend image gets `VITE_API_URL` as a build arg, and the value depends on the compose file. In `compose.yml` (production) it is `https://api.${DOMAIN}`, and the build fails if `DOMAIN` isn't set. In `compose.override.yml` (local development) it is `http://localhost:8000`. The override file also builds a separate playwright image with `http://backend:8000`, but that isn't the frontend image.

In nginx.conf, `location /` serves static files from /usr/share/nginx/html with `try_files $uri /index.html =404`. A path that isn't a real file falls back to /index.html, so SPA deep links load the app and the client router handles them. The same config includes /etc/nginx/extra-conf.d/*.conf. In the frontend container, nginx-backend-not-found.conf supplies that include. It defines `location /api`, `/docs` and `/redoc`, and each one does `return 404`. Those paths therefore return a plain 404 and don't fall back to index.html. I didn't check the Dockerfile to confirm how the file is mounted into extra-conf.d.

The external Docker network `traefik-public` must exist first. Create it on the remote server with `docker network create traefik-public`. Traefik uses it to talk to your stack(s). Both compose files declare it as `external: true`.

The dashboard is enabled with `--api` and exposed through Traefik's internal `api@internal` service. It is served at `traefik.${DOMAIN}` by an HTTPS router (`traefik-dashboard-https`) on the `https` entrypoint (port 443). That router uses TLS with Let's Encrypt certificates from the `le` resolver. A separate HTTP router on port 80 only redirects to HTTPS, using the permanent `https-redirect` middleware. The HTTPS router is protected by the `admin-auth` HTTP Basic Auth middleware. Its credentials come from the required `USERNAME` and `HASHED_PASSWORD` environment variables.

Give the staging runner the label `staging`. The workflow's `runs-on` is `[self-hosted, staging]`, so the runner must be self-hosted and carry that label. You add the label when the runner setup asks about labels, or you can add it later. A push or merge to the `master` branch triggers the "Deploy to Staging" workflow, which runs on that runner. It only runs in user projects, because of the `github.repository_owner != 'fastapi'` condition. The workflow also needs these repo secrets: DOMAIN_STAGING, STACK_NAME_STAGING, SECRET_KEY, FIRST_SUPERUSER, FIRST_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, EMAILS_FROM_EMAIL, and the SMTP and Sentry ones.

For the backend service, `docker compose watch` syncs the `./backend` directory into `/app/backend` in the container, ignoring `./backend/.venv` and `.venv`. It rebuilds the service when `./backend/pyproject.toml` changes.

It's a smoke test that the stack builds and starts. It runs on pushes to master and on PRs (opened/synchronize). It runs `docker compose build`, then `down -v`, then `up -d --wait backend frontend adminer`. It then curls the backend health-check (http://localhost:8000/api/v1/utils/health-check) and the frontend (http://localhost:5173), and finally tears everything down. It runs no unit tests.

compose.override.yml (the local stack) publishes these host ports: 80 (Traefik proxy, mapped to container 80), 8090 (Traefik dashboard, mapped to container 8080), 5432 (Postgres db), 8080 (adminer), 8000 (backend), 1080 (mailcatcher web UI), 1025 (mailcatcher SMTP), 5173 (frontend, mapped to container 80) and 9323 (Playwright report). compose.traefik.yml separately publishes 80 and 443, but it is not part of the local override.

No. The unauthenticated create-user endpoint (POST /private/users/) is only registered when settings.ENVIRONMENT == "local". Production deploys set ENVIRONMENT=production (deploy-production.yml), so the private router isn't mounted there. Caveat: ENVIRONMENT defaults to "local", so a deployment that fails to set it would expose it.

In the Test Backend workflow, only the supporting services run in containers. `docker compose up -d db mailcatcher` starts the database and the mailcatcher. The rest runs directly on the ubuntu-latest runner, not in a container. That covers checkout, Python setup, uv install, the DB migration (`uv run bash scripts/prestart.sh`), the tests (`scripts/tests-start.sh`), the coverage report, and the artifact upload. The backend app and tests use the runner's Python through uv. The containers are torn down with `docker compose down -v --remove-orphans` before and after the tests.

Yes. In local development the included Traefik proxy exposes its web UI/dashboard at http://localhost:8090. The compose.override.yml maps port 8090 to 8080 and enables --api.insecure=true. The UI shows how the proxy handles routes. In production the dashboard is at https://traefik.<domain>.

Yes. Stop the backend container with `docker compose stop backend`. Then run `cd backend` and `fastapi dev app/main.py`, which reloads on code changes. The local server uses port 8000, the same port the Docker backend used. The frontend and the other services in Docker keep working without any changes.

Install the prek git hook in your local repo. From the `backend` folder, run `uv run prek install -f`. This writes the hook to `.git/hooks/pre-commit`, and the `-f` flag overwrites any existing pre-commit hook. After that, prek runs the checks from `.pre-commit-config.yaml` on every `git commit`. If it reformats files, stage them again with `git add` and commit again. prek is already a project dependency.

Open a shell in the backend container with `docker compose exec backend bash`. Then run `alembic revision --autogenerate -m "Add column last_name to User model"` to create the migration. Alembic is already set up to read the models in backend/app/models.py. Commit the generated files in the alembic directory. Apply the migration with `alembic upgrade head`.

In the local `.env` file, set `DOMAIN=localhost.tiangolo.com`, then re-run `docker compose watch`. The included Traefik in `compose.override.yml` will route `api.localhost.tiangolo.com` to the backend and `dashboard.localhost.tiangolo.com` to the frontend. That domain and all its subdomains resolve to 127.0.0.1, so you don't need to edit /etc/hosts.

Yes. The repo has a ready-made VS Code launch config with two debug configurations. One runs the FastAPI backend under debugpy with uvicorn (app.main:app --reload, cwd backend, envFile .env). The other launches Chrome against http://localhost:5173 for the frontend.

The report is the HTML coverage report at `htmlcov/index.html`. `backend/scripts/test.sh` generates it with `coverage html`, and inside the container it ends up at `/app/backend/htmlcov`. You can open it from your host. `compose.override.yml` bind-mounts `./backend/htmlcov` to `/app/backend/htmlcov` for the backend service. After a run, open `backend/htmlcov/index.html` in your browser. The mount is marked with a TODO to remove it once coverage is done locally.

The `prestart` container (compose.yml, `command: bash scripts/prestart.sh`) runs backend/scripts/prestart.sh. That script waits for the DB, then runs `alembic upgrade head`, which creates the tables through the migrations. It then runs `python app/initial_data.py`, which calls `init_db` in app/core/db.py. `init_db` creates the first superuser from FIRST_SUPERUSER and FIRST_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD if that user doesn't already exist. The line that creates the admin is the `crud.create_user` call in db.py, and the tables come from the `alembic upgrade head` line in prestart.sh.

Open the "Appearance" menu (sun/moon/monitor button, in the sidebar or on the auth pages) and choose "Light". Yes, it's remembered. setTheme writes the choice to localStorage under the key "vite-ui-theme" (set in main.tsx). On the next load the ThemeProvider reads it back. The default is dark if nothing has been saved.

The label-checker requires exactly one of: breaking, security, feature, bug, refactor, upgrade, docs, lang-all, internal. Ask a maintainer to add whichever fits your PR (e.g. `bug` for a fix, `feature` for new functionality, `docs` for documentation).

No. Merging to master only deploys to staging (per deployment.md). Production deploys only when a GitHub release is published (the workflow triggers on `release: published`). So your change goes live in production only after someone publishes a release. Also, the production job is skipped in the main fastapi repo and only runs in user projects.
